original_question: Let K be the Kasteleyn matrix of an a, b, c semiregular hexagon, and let the associated Carlitz matrix be the b-by-b matrix obtained from K by row and column reductions, with entries given by binomial coefficients. Determine the cokernel of these Carlitz matrices, equivalently the cokernel of the Kasteleyn matrices of a, b, c hexagons, and if possible interpret that cokernel in terms of lozenge tilings.
target_in_paper: Section 2 ("Lozenges"), Problem 5: determine the cokernel of the Carlitz matrix, equivalently of the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the a,b,c semiregular hexagon, and if possible interpret that cokernel in terms of the tilings.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper-faithful target. It correctly identifies the lozenge-tiling setting of an a,b,c semiregular hexagon, the passage from the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix to a Carlitz matrix by row and column reduction, the fact that the relevant invariant is the cokernel, the equivalence between the Carlitz and Kasteleyn-Percus formulations, and the paper’s optional second clause asking for a tiling-theoretic interpretation.
missing_details: The paper works with the a,b,c semiregular hexagon having side lengths a,b,c,a,b,c, with a,b,c positive integers and all angles 120 degrees.

The matrix in the paper is the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the finite honeycomb graph dual to that hexagon; in this honeycomb case, no sign changes are needed, so one may take the ordinary bipartite adjacency matrix.
The Carlitz matrix should be specified as the integer b-by-b matrix C_{a,b,c} with entries C_{ij} = (a+c choose a+i-j) for 1 <= i,j <= b.
The cokernel is over the integers: coker(C_{a,b,c}) = Z^b / im(C_{a,b,c}) (equivalently for the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix), viewed as a finite abelian group.
The equivalence between the Carlitz and Kasteleyn-Percus formulations comes from integral row and column reductions, which the paper explicitly notes do not change the cokernel.
Nearby context notes that permuting a,b,c gives three different Carlitz matrices with the same cokernel; the problem is really about this common cokernel.
To make the question stand alone, the lozenge-tiling side should be tied explicitly to matchings of the dual finite honeycomb graph.
refined_question: For positive integers a,b,c, let H(a,b,c) be the semiregular hexagon with side lengths a,b,c,a,b,c, and let K_{a,b,c} be the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the finite honeycomb graph dual to H(a,b,c) (equivalently here, the ordinary bipartite adjacency matrix). Let C_{a,b,c} be the integer b-by-b Carlitz matrix obtained from K_{a,b,c} by integral row and column reductions, with (i,j)-entry C_{ij} = (a+c choose a+i-j). Determine the finite abelian group coker_Z(C_{a,b,c}) = Z^b / im(C_{a,b,c}) — equivalently coker_Z(K_{a,b,c}), and hence the common cokernel of the three Carlitz matrices arising from permuting a,b,c — and, if possible, give a direct interpretation of this cokernel in terms of lozenge tilings (equivalently matchings) of H(a,b,c).
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: determine, over Z, the cokernel of the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the finite honeycomb graph dual to the a,b,c semiregular hexagon, and if possible interpret that group in terms of the lozenge tilings of the hexagon.
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of the paper’s Section 2, Problem 5. The nearby setup first defines the a,b,c semiregular hexagon and identifies its lozenge tilings with matchings of the dual honeycomb graph. It then states that systematic row and column reduction of the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix yields the b-by-b Carlitz matrix with entries (a+c choose a+i-j), and explicitly says that these reductions do not change the cokernel, understood as an abelian group whose order is the determinant. The same paragraph adds the permutation symmetry in a,b,c, producing three nontrivially different Carlitz matrices with the same cokernel. The official problem statement is therefore exactly the cokernel-determination problem together with the optional request for a tiling interpretation; it is not a broader question about arbitrary planar graphs or about other matrix invariants. The examples c=1 (cyclic cokernel) and a=b=c=2 (noncyclic cokernel Z/2Z x Z/10Z) are contextual motivation, not part of the formal statement.
